tagline.text: An easy-to-reach four-tier waterfall in Bato, Catanduanes

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangays Marinawa and Binanwahan, Bato, Catanduanes

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,000 (fees, transport and meals, rough estimate from Virac)

children.text: Maribina Falls is a waterfall in Bato, Catanduanes, reached on foot from the main road. Its several tiers and pools make it one of the island's best-known places for swimming and relaxing.
Maribina Falls is a waterfall in Bato, Catanduanes. Its name is said to combine one syllable each from the two barangays it spans, Marinawa and Binanwahan. One travel blog says it is about
1km
off the main road and just a few kilometers from both Virac and Bato. Bato is a municipality in the southeast, about
8km

from the provincial capital Virac, and one reader's comment calls this falls one of the most popular and accessible on the island. Catanduanes is an island province east of the Bicol region, with an area of about 1,492 sq km and a 2024 population of about 261,169. Its coastline is nearly 400 km long, it has 11 municipalities and 315 barangays, and it carries the nickname Land of the Howling Winds. Fully open to the Philippine Sea, it is frequently hit by typhoons, but that is also what makes its waves and scenery rugged and distinctive.

The falls is a stepped cascade of several tiers. One blog wrote that there are four major cascades, with the top one the highest and fullest, water dropping into a deep pool and then flowing into a shallower pool below. There is said to be a large boulder between the third and fourth cascades. Heights differ by source: one says about 5–6 m and one reader's comment says about 5 m. Understand it as a modest fall of a size good for cooling off and playing, not a very high one.

The surroundings feel more like a tidy resort than deep jungle. There are cemented paths, cottages and a small store, and one guide says there is no restaurant and only one sari-sari store. Many reviews say the water is very cold, which suits swimming on hot days. Some guides say the falls are near the trailhead for Mt. Lantad, but the condition of any route from the falls to the mountain could not be confirmed. The town of Bato is known to have been founded in 1799, has a 2024 population of about 21,325, and is made up of 27 barangays. The Bato River divides the town into east and west districts, and the elevation climbs from sea level to about 700 m.

plus an environmental fee of

, which match what a blog lists for another Bato attraction (Binurong Point), so treat them as uncertain for this waterfall. Another review said a guide is mandatory, but recent guides do not mention one. One source even says there is no entrance fee. The most accurate approach is to confirm with the Bato tourism desk or your lodging just before you visit. The differences probably arise because the surveys were done at different times and the local government may charge usage and environmental fees separately. Whether a guide is required also seems to vary over time, so get a receipt on the spot and check that the amount matches the official notice.

There are four large cascades, with the top one the biggest. Water runs from the upper pool to the lower pool, and one review described adults at the first pool and children at the second. On weekday afternoons it is said to be less crowded.
Many comments say the water is cool and clear, good for cooling off on a hot day. Some people jump from the rocks, but jumping without checking the depth and the bottom yourself is dangerous.

blocks.title: Easy on-foot access from the main road

children.text: You walk about 15 minutes in from the main road, past concrete houses, a small bridge and abaca drying by the roadside. The last stretch is uphill. You can also go by tricycle or habal-habal to the entrance. During the 15-minute walk you see village life, so it doubles as a short stroll and a look at the village. Strollers and wheelchairs may be difficult because of the final climb.

blocks.title: Cottages and a place to rest

children.text: Concrete cottages are reported, and one older review said a cottage was
each. It is convenient for families to rest and eat packed lunches, but confirm current rates and usage rules locally.

blocks.title: Pair it with the old church in Bato

children.text: One blog introduces the old church in Bato along with the falls. The Bato River divides the town east and west, and Wikipedia says the Bato Bridge is the longest in the Bicol region.

blocks.title: A day trip close to Virac

children.text: Bato is about 8 km from Virac, so you can base yourself in Virac and make it a half-day trip. Adding a nearby beach or another sight after the falls fills out the day.

blocks.title: One stop on an island itinerary

children.text: Catanduanes is known for its wave-battered Pacific coast, caves and waterfalls. Maribina Falls is a good place to rest on an island loop. Puraran Beach is known for good surf from July to October, and places such as Luyang Cave Park in San Andres, Nahulugan Falls in Gigmoto, San Miguel River Park (tubing and kayaking), Bato Church and the Batalay Holy Cross Shrine, and the Museo de Catanduanes in Virac are listed as island candidates. If you have time, it is better to use Virac as a base and tour the island for two days or more.

items.title: Half day from Virac
items.subtitle: Swim at the falls, then lunch

children.text: From your Virac lodging, take a jeepney or tricycle toward Bato. It is about 8 km.
Walk about 15 minutes from the main road to the falls entrance. Check the entrance fee and guide rules.
See the falls from the first pool up to the top and swim.
Eat your packed lunch or go to a nearby restaurant. There is reportedly no restaurant at the falls.
Go into Bato town and look around the old church.
Right after rain the water can rise and become dangerous, so check the weather first.

items.title: A day in Catanduanes
items.subtitle: The falls and a drive along the island's east

children.text: Hire a motorcycle or car in Virac.
Swim and rest at Maribina Falls.
Have lunch in Bato town and head toward the island's east coast.
Return to Virac before sunset.
For the island's east coast, see the Catanduanes and Binurong Point entries as well.
The gateway to Catanduanes is Virac Airport (VRC). Flights from Manila to Virac vary by airline and date, so check the latest schedule.
There is also a way to enter Catanduanes by boat from a port on mainland Bicol. Check boat times and fares locally.
From Virac to Bato is about
8km
. You go by jeepney, tricycle or habal-habal, and one blog wrote that from the main road to the falls entrance a tricycle was
and public transport then walking was about
(old information).
From the main road to the falls is about
15 minutes
on foot, with the last stretch uphill.
See also the Catanduanes entry for general information.
To see the island's east as well, it is easier to hire a motorcycle or vehicle in Virac.
After a typhoon, road conditions can change, so check local news.

Catanduanes has no pronounced dry season, with annual rainfall of about 2,619 mm over roughly 112 rainy days. Wikipedia explains that March–August is relatively dry, October to early January is the coolest and rainiest period, and March–May is the hottest. A waterfall is more impressive when the water is plentiful, but right after heavy rain the current gets strong and the paths slippery, which is dangerous. March–August is the more comfortable time for swimming. The water is cold all year, so it is especially popular in hot weather.
Catanduanes is an island in the path of typhoons. Super Typhoon Goni (locally Rolly) made landfall in Bato on November 1, 2020, so leave some slack in your plans during typhoon season.

Lodgings are concentrated in Virac town, so there are few choices in Bato or near the falls. Staying in Virac and making a half-day trip is usual; check prices and vacancies by date on a booking site.

There is no restaurant at the falls, only about a sari-sari store, so bring a packed lunch and water. Have lunch in Bato town or in Virac. Island food is basically seafood and Bicol dishes made with coconut milk. Bring plenty of cash.

Catanduanes is also famous as a producer of abaca (Manila hemp), so it is common to see abaca drying by the roadside. An Abaca Festival in the fourth week of May and the Catandungan Festival on October 24–26, marking the island's independence, are reported. If your dates match, enjoy them too. Event schedules can change from year to year, so check the latest announcements.
Fee and guide rules differ between sources, so check locally first.
Bring swimwear, a towel, a change of clothes and non-slip shoes (aqua shoes).
Do not go on a day of heavy rain. The current can suddenly get strong.
Weekday afternoons tend to be quiet. Weekends and holidays can be crowded.
Bring packed food, water and a trash bag, and take your trash back.
Put valuables in a waterproof bag and do not leave them in the cottage.
Put your camera or phone in a waterproof case.
The Bato river bridge and Bato Church make good photo spots and are worth a short stop before or after the falls.
Facilities may have been repaired since Super Typhoon Goni in 2020, so check the current state when you visit.
Right after heavy rain and in typhoon season the current at the falls gets strong and the rocks are slippery. Check the depth and the bottom before swimming, and keep children with adults.
When jumping from rocks, check the depth and hidden rocks yourself.
Wet rocks and moss are extremely slippery.
Fees and guide requirements differ between sources, so check before you visit to avoid needless disputes.
After a typhoon, paths and facilities may be in a different condition.
There is no first-aid facility near the falls, so carry your own emergency medicine.
Do not simply trust the fees and information in old reviews; check the official fee list at the entrance.
